title: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
summary:
Remote Desktop Protocol is a Microsoft protocol that provides graphical remote access to a Windows session, and it is one of the most common lateral movement mechanisms because it is enabled by default on many server builds and requires only valid credentials and reachable network access. An adversary who has obtained credentials or a session token can authenticate to a target host, interact with the desktop as the compromised identity, and from that host repeat the process toward further systems. The same protocol is used for legitimate administration and remote work, which is why detection depends on context, direction of travel, and authentication characteristics rather than on the protocol itself.

Events are recorded on both ends. The source host shows a client process and outbound connection to the destination port, while the destination host records the logon with a network logon type, the source address, and often a dedicated operational log for connection and session events that captures the connecting account, address, and session identifiers. Where a gateway or jump host mediates access, gateway logs supply the external source address and may reveal whether the connection was brokered by a known administrative path. Additional artefacts include the creation of user profile directories on first logon, drive and clipboard redirection activity, and any process spawned from the session.

Benign remote desktop traffic is extremely heavy in most estates, frequently originating from administrative subnets and management platforms. Investigations look at whether the destination host is one this account or this source normally reaches, whether the connection occurred outside a change window, whether the authentication used a local or domain account that should not be used interactively on that host, and what happened immediately after the session began. Compromised sessions frequently exhibit short dwell time, tool execution, and a rapid sequence of connections to additional hosts using the same credentials.
objectives: Explain how network logon types, session identifiers, and connection logs combine to identify remote desktop access to a host.
Correlate source-side client process telemetry with destination-side authentication records to confirm a session.
Distinguish bastion and administrative remote desktop use from adversary lateral movement using baseline direction and account norms.
Analyse authentication anomalies such as local account usage, unusual logon hours, and first-seen source to destination pairs.
Describe the evidence available when a session is brokered through a gateway or jump host and how it changes scoping.
Map remote desktop lateral movement to ATT&CK and specify the mitigation controls that constrain it most effectively.

beginner.definition: Remote Desktop Protocol is a feature built into Windows that lets you see and control another computer's screen over a network. You log in with a real account, and it feels like you are sitting at that machine. Security teams shorten the name to RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol).
beginner.whyItMatters: If an attacker steals one password, remote desktop can carry them from a laptop to a server in a single step. Many servers turn the feature on by default, so there is often nothing to break. The traffic is encrypted and looks like normal administration. This makes it one of the most common ways intruders spread sideways through a network.
howItWorks: An attacker already has a working username and password for one account on the network.
They open a remote desktop connection to a server they can reach from the internet or the network.
The server checks the password and starts a session, so the attacker now controls that desktop.
Everything the attacker does runs as that account, so their actions look like a normal login.
From that server they repeat the same trick toward the next machine, one hop at a time.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel where every room key also opens the staff office. A thief who finds one key card in the car park can walk in the front door, then step into the back office, then open the storeroom. Nothing looks broken and no alarm sounds, because the key is genuine. Remote desktop works the same way. One stolen password becomes a real login, and the intruder simply keeps opening doors that were never meant for them.
takeaways: Remote desktop is a real login, so watch who connects to which server and when.
Limit which accounts may use it, and force administrators through one controlled jump host.
Log both ends of a session, because one side shows the request and the other shows the access.
